segments.heading: Abstract
segments.text: Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of condylar head fractures (CHF) can be challenging. Virtual planning and CAD/CAM-based patient-specific devices (PSD) offer to enhance the accuracy of fragment reduction. We present four CHF cases demonstrating the strengths and shortcomings of different PSD designs. From this still limited experience, some fundamental recommendations evolved: • The PSD design should permit adequate visualization of the fracture line to ensure anatomical fracture reduction. • The PSD for reposition and prefixation of the medial fragment should incorporate an abundance of screw holes, particularly in its lateral section, since this part is most easily accessible intraoperatively. • PSDs extended over the dome of the condylar head should be omitted to avoid interferences between fragments, PSD and the adjacent glenoid fossa.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Mandibular condylar head fractures (CHF) can be treated non-surgically or through open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) []. ORIF is the preferred modality when the CHF lines are located within or below the lateral pole zone of the condyle and accompanied by dislocation of the medial fragment, resulting in loss of the vertical ramus height []. ORIF has been demonstrated to provide superior morphological and functional outcomes compared to non-surgical therapy of CHF [–].
segments.text_with_reference_markers: Mandibular condylar head fractures (CHF) can be treated non-surgically or through open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) [ [BIBR:CR1 1] ]. ORIF is the preferred modality when the CHF lines are located within or below the lateral pole zone of the condyle and accompanied by dislocation of the medial fragment, resulting in loss of the vertical ramus height [ [BIBR:CR2 2] ]. ORIF has been demonstrated to provide superior morphological and functional outcomes compared to non-surgical therapy of CHF [ [BIBR:CR3 3] – [BIBR:CR5 5] ].

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Various techniques for ORIF of CHF were described in the literature including microplates, miniplates, lag screws and positional screws [–]. Lateral small-fragment positional screw osteosynthesis (LSFPSO) has shown good functional and stable long-term outcomes []. Still, accurate reduction and fixation of the medial bone portions may be demanding above all in major fragmentation [].

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Virtual surgical planning (VSP) and computer-aided design/ computer-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM) PSDs provide high accuracy for reduction of bone segments or fragments and are current best practice in orthognathic surgery and post-trauma or oncologic reconstruction of the facial skeleton [–].

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: This case series (from 2017 to 2020) reviews PSDs for ORIF of CHF, analyses their advantages and limitations, and suggests design refinements to overcome identified drawbacks.

segments.heading: Case 1
segments.text: 38-year-old male with bilateral mandibular CHF and a symphyseal fracture resulting from interpersonal violence.

segments.heading: Case 1 / Clinical Findings
segments.text: Limited jaw opening, bilateral preauricular swelling, malocclusion, frontal open bite.

segments.heading: Case 1 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: High-resolution (0.625 mm) Computed Tomography (CT) revealed bilateral CHF, both lateral to the lateral pole zone (AO type-p) (Table 1) with lost vertical apposition, no fragmentation on the right, and minor fragmentation on the left (Fig. 1).
segments.text_with_reference_markers: High-resolution (0.625 mm) Computed Tomography (CT) revealed bilateral CHF, both lateral to the lateral pole zone (AO type-p) (Table [TABLE:Tab1 1] ) with lost vertical apposition, no fragmentation on the right, and minor fragmentation on the left (Fig. [FIG:Fig1 1] ).

segments.heading: Case 1 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: Interactive VSP with an industrial partner (KLS Martin Group, Tuttlingen, Germany) went for a PSD design to assist anatomical fracture reduction of the medial condylar fragment and prefixation prior to definitive fixation with a two screw LSFPSO. The PSDs were intended for removal at the operation’s conclusion.

segments.heading: Case 1 / Implant Design
segments.text: The PSD design featured a solid rhomboid shield in the upper part for reduction and prefixation of the medial fragment, transitioning into a curved lower end below the fracture line for fixation along the lateral surface of the ramus. Multiple holes enabled flexibility for optimal screw placement, accommodating emerging access limitations or compromised bone quality.

segments.heading: Case 1 / Surgical Procedure
segments.text: The symphyseal fracture underwent ORIF with two miniplates. The right CHF was exposed through a preauricular approach. The medial condylar fragment, displaced antero-caudo-medially, was reduced by means of sharp hooks and diamond-coated elevators. The placement of the PSD obstructed the fracture line with its rhomboid shield, necessitating a change in strategy. Instead of the PSD a grid plate (1.2 mm screws; Medartis AG, Basel, Switzerland) was used for prefixation of the medial fragment after anatomical reduction. The PSD was then placed onto the plate and mounted (1.2 mm screws) for reinforcement. Two small-fragment screws (1.8 mm, Medartis) were inserted in typical LSFPSO manner. The left-side ORIF with the second PSD was deferred because a reproducible multipoint occlusion had been achieved via reduction of the right condylar head.

segments.heading: Case 1 / Outcome
segments.text: Postoperative Panorex confirmed adequate reduction and fixation. Functional treatment with elastics was performed for three weeks.

segments.heading: Case 2
segments.text: 13-year-old boy with a right mandibular CHF caused by a fall.

segments.heading: Case 2 / Clinical Findings
segments.text: Limited jaw opening, contralateral open bite.

segments.heading: Case 2 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: CT imaging revealed an AO type-p CHF with no fragmentation but lost vertical apposition. The medial fragment exhibited an atypical rectangular shape and was displaced antero-medially and angulated caudally (Fig. 2).
segments.text_with_reference_markers: CT imaging revealed an AO type-p CHF with no fragmentation but lost vertical apposition. The medial fragment exhibited an atypical rectangular shape and was displaced antero-medially and angulated caudally (Fig. [FIG:Fig2 2] ).

segments.heading: Case 2 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: VSP mirrored the contralateral condylar head to define the pre-injury position of the fragment as foundation for the PSD design. This approach was comfortable but ignored the unique shape of the medial fragment and the fracture line’s course, eventually leading to suboptimal PSD fit.

segments.heading: Case 2 / Implant Design
segments.text: A P-shaped PSD with three screw holes for dorsal fixation of the medial fragment and additional holes for lateral neck fixation was designed. Angulated insertion points for two positional screws were incorporated. The PSD allowed for visualization of the fracture line; removal at the end of the operation was planned.

segments.heading: Case 2 / Surgical Procedure
segments.text: The PSD bridged the fracture. The fragment’s flat configuration allowed LSFPSO with one screw (1.8 mm, length:15 mm; Medartis) only. Consequently, the PSD was left in situ as stand-by to reinforce overall stability.

segments.heading: Case 2 / Outcome
segments.text: Postoperative CT confirmed proper reduction and fixation.

segments.heading: Case 2 / Outcome
segments.text: Elastics were used for 10 days. At seven months postoperatively, bony consolidation was observed, though screw and plate loosening necessitated hardware removal. Preinjury occlusion was stable, and jaw opening unrestricted.

segments.heading: Case 3
segments.text: 59-year-old woman after right CHF, initially treated non-surgically.

segments.heading: Case 3 / Clinical Findings
segments.text: Malocclusion, right temporomandibular joint pain 16 months post injury.

segments.heading: Case 3 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: Imaging revealed deformation of the right condylar head with vertical ramus height loss due to medial fragment displacement (Fig. 3). VSP led to the implementation of a crescent-shaped osteotomy for mobilization and reduction of the medial segment and PSD-assisted fixation. The virtual reduction of the medial fragment produced an osteotomy gap.
segments.text_with_reference_markers: Imaging revealed deformation of the right condylar head with vertical ramus height loss due to medial fragment displacement (Fig. [FIG:Fig3 3] ). VSP led to the implementation of a crescent-shaped osteotomy for mobilization and reduction of the medial segment and PSD-assisted fixation. The virtual reduction of the medial fragment produced an osteotomy gap.

segments.heading: Case 3 / Implant Design
segments.text: Due to this gap a large-scale, rigid P-shaped PSD was designed with a fenestration to inspect the osteotomy gap, multiple screw holes for bony anchoring and LSFPSO indicators. The upper arm contained 3 screw receiving holes. The lower arm descended on the posterior surface of the condylar process with a curvature below the level of the sigmoid notch to create enough space for five screw holes. The principal load bearing function relied on the LSFPSO. The optimal entry points for two respective screws were indicated by triangular laser-etched notches in the lower arm of the PSD.

segments.heading: Case 3 / Surgical Procedure
segments.text: A piezosurgery osteotomy was performed, and the medial condylar segment was repositioned into the glenoid fossa. The PSD was applied uneventfully. Owing to poor bone quality, prefixation of the medial segment with a screw was limited to the uppermost PSD hole. As anticipated an irregular gap remained between the segments. The upper screw for the LSPSO could be inserted guided by the notch indicator. Since the form of the bony gap differed from VSP due to the material reduction during piezosurgical sawing the second screw was inserted free hand antero-superiorly of the indicating notch and angulated in a vertical direction to safely purchase the medial fragment.

segments.heading: Case 3 / Outcome
segments.text: X-rays confirmed adequate reduction of the condylar head, proper location in the glenoid fossa and restored vertical ramus height.

segments.heading: Case 3 / Outcome
segments.text: Six months postoperatively, the patient developed right-sided preauricular pain and restricted jaw opening. CT-Imaging revealed a contact of the PSD with the glenoid fossa. Hardware removal alleviated symptoms, and further follow-up was unremarkable.

segments.heading: Case 4
segments.text: 62-year-old man with left mandibular multi-fragmented CHF following a bike accident.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Clinical Findings
segments.text: Severe occlusal disturbances, ipsilateral open bite.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: CT-Scans delineated a left AO type-p CHF with multi-fragmentation (three major fragments), loss of vertical apposition, and anteromedial displacement (Fig. 4).
segments.text_with_reference_markers: CT-Scans delineated a left AO type-p CHF with multi-fragmentation (three major fragments), loss of vertical apposition, and anteromedial displacement (Fig. [FIG:Fig4 4] ).

segments.heading: Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: A three-component multi-purpose PSD was designed. In line with previous cases, one PSD component of the PSD was designated to reduction and prefixation. To address the difficulties in stabilizing the dislocated largest medial fragment alongside smaller pieces, the upper PSD portion was equipped with four finger-like extensions along the entire posterior surface of the condylar head. The middle section of the PSD incorporated a large window for unobstructed visualization of the fracture line and its cranial ramifications. The lower PSD portion encompassed the neck region, reaching down to the level of the deepest point of the sigmoid notch. Its anterior border contained an undulating recess serving as docking site for the second PSD component, i.e. a “tandem” washer for load distribution and reinforcement of the LSFPSO.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: The upper PSD portion included six screw holes arranged in two rows (four along the common arch brace and one on each of the two central dome extensions) to ensure adequate fixation of the reassembled fragments, even if not every screw hole was occupied. The lower PSD portion contained three screw holes in a triangular configuration for anchoring to the condylar neck and base region.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: The PSD “tandem” washer seated within the lateral recess along the first PSD component. This second PSD combined washer and navigation function: the tongue-in-groove design of the two components ensured accurate intraoperative transfer of the LSFPSO entry points onto the lateral fracture end at the ramus. Besides the two washer screw holes the PSD contained a third smaller hole for its temporary fixation during LSFPSO.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: Detachable drill guides, designed to indicate the angulation and intramedullary pathways for the LSFPSO screws within the medial fragment assembly, were provided in two versions: two separate metallic cylinders joined by a polymer sleeve with and without a long rod-like handle.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
segments.text: The PSD tool set was complemented with a third component, a small T-shaped implant to augment the rigidity of the overall reconstruction after removal of the primary (reduction/prefixation) PSD. The T-shaped PSD was conceived to link the condylar neck and head and retain the small intermediate dorsal monocortical fragment (SIDMF) at the posterior condylar surface.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Surgical Procedure
segments.text: The dislocated major dome fragment, along with the smaller medial fragments, were successfully reassembled and anatomically reduced. However, repeated attempts to position the reduction/prefixation PSD component as pre-planned failed. Unresolvable collisions between the dome fragment, the cranial PSD extensions and the glenoid fossa hindered the first component from bypassing the bony crest and slipping into its planned final position.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Surgical Procedure
segments.text: For salvage the large medial condylar head fragment was reduced and fixated to the lateral fracture end with a conventional grid plate (1.2 mm screws; Medartis). To achieve this, it became necessary to remove the SIDMF and to close the interfragmentary gap by a slight pitch movement. This adjustment was required because the available grid plate was too short.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Surgical Procedure
segments.text: The entry points for the LSFPSO were established with the aid of the washer PSD. Despite the discrepancies from VSP, the placement of the washer components, drill guides and drilling could be carried out with sufficient precision. Because the bone surrounding the drill holes did not necessitate load distribution the washer PSD was removed prior to insertion of two screws (1.8 mm screws; Medartis) for the LSFPSO.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Surgical Procedure
segments.text: Occlusion and latero-/protrusion movements were assessed intraoperatively and confirmed satisfactory fracture reduction and stabilisation. Consequently, the grid plate was removed. Minimisation of the residual gap and SIDMF replantation were deemed unnecessary. Further stabilization with the T-shaped PSD was also not pursued.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Outcome
segments.text: A postoperative panoramic X-ray confirmed anatomical reduction of the fracture.

segments.heading: Case 4 / Outcome
segments.text: Clinical Follow up: asymptomatic with unimpaired function.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: LSFPSO using two or three screws has emerged as the most popular surgical treatment modality for CHF [, ]. The concept of combining PSDs with screw fixation might offer a promising approach for treating challenging CHF up to most troublesome multifragment patterns [].
segments.text_with_reference_markers: LSFPSO using two or three screws has emerged as the most popular surgical treatment modality for CHF [ [BIBR:CR2 2] , [BIBR:CR6 6] ]. The concept of combining PSDs with screw fixation might offer a promising approach for treating challenging CHF up to most troublesome multifragment patterns [ [BIBR:CR13 13] ].

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Pavlychuk et al. have outlined sophisticated CAD/CAM PSD designs to support ORIF of CHFs across three publications [–]. For unclear reasons, their concept has not met much resonance in the literature so far. Our case series showcases the intraoperative constraints encountered with three single-component and one multi-component PSD, the latter inspired by Pavlychuk et al.

segments.heading: Discussion / Roles and Advantages of PSD in CHFs
segments.text: PSDs are used alongside LSFPSO. PSDs can be tailored to perform multiple functions, including:

segments.heading: Discussion / Roles and Advantages of PSD in CHFs
segments.text: Assist reduction, reassembly and prefixation of medial condylar head fragments. Navigate LSFPSO entry points. Guide drilling for intramedullary screw placement (LSFPSO). Augment osteosynthesis rigidity through reinforcement.

segments.heading: Discussion / Roles and Advantages of PSD in CHFs
segments.text: PSDs may be employed intraoperatively only or retained for long-term stability. Their advantages over off-the-shelf hardware include improved fragment reduction accuracy, enhanced rigidity, and reduced operative time, as evidenced in other surgical contexts [, ].
segments.text_with_reference_markers: PSDs may be employed intraoperatively only or retained for long-term stability. Their advantages over off-the-shelf hardware include improved fragment reduction accuracy, enhanced rigidity, and reduced operative time, as evidenced in other surgical contexts [ [BIBR:CR10 10] , [BIBR:CR11 11] ].

segments.heading: Discussion / Insights from this Case Series
segments.text: A principal cause for the pitfalls described above was limited experience with nuanced PSD design features for CHF management. Crucially, salvage solutions were at hand in all cases. To flatten the learning curve in order to establish and help to disseminate PSDs in surgical CHF treatment, we would like to refer to the following recommendations and caveats for the PSD design:

segments.heading: Discussion / Insights from this Case Series
segments.text: VSP–Fracture Line Analysis: Accurate analysis of the fracture line and reduction of fragments in the planning phase is essential – rather than simply relying on mirroring and superimposition of intact contralateral structures. Mandibular asymmetry will compromise the true morphology and course of fracture lines []. Intraoperative Visualization: Ensure a reliable overview of the entire fracture line course during every phase of the surgical intervention by incorporating large fenestrations or cross-bracings into the PSD design. This principle has been repeatedly exemplified in wire-frame patient-specific cutting guides [, ]. Flexible Strategies for Screw Fixation: Provide an excess of drilling/ screw−receiving holes in the PSD design, even if only the most suitable subset of the surplus of screw holes may be occupied to deal with unforeseen problems, such as poor bone quality or inaccessible anatomic sites. The integration of screw holes in excess numbers into osteosynthesis plates designs to increase intraoperative flexibility has already been described in context with condylar base and neck fractures []. Thoughtfully executed Coverage across Relevant Anatomical Sites: Extend the PSD to encompass the infero−lateral surface of the medial condylar head fragment approaching to the margin of the fracture line. This is an easily accessible area, which facilitates screw insertion besides control of accurate reduction of the inferior part of the fracture. Temporary Use of Grid Plates: Remove grid plates or medial fragment−reduction PSD component after LSFPSO is secured unless a “stand−by” stabilization is required.

segments.heading: Discussion / Insights from this Case Series
segments.text: Loosening of positional screws and conventional grid plates is a known issue in ORIF of CHF []. Possible causes include poor bone quality or cyclic loading, leading to the backout of screws []. Therefore, a grid plate or PSD should be removed subsequent to the LSFPSO to preclude a secondary hardware removal. An exception is the need for additional stabilization via “standby” with extrabony fixation devices.

segments.heading: Discussion / Case-specific Insights and Recommendations
segments.text: At the treatment time of Case 4, we have been overly enthusiastic in adopting ideas from the novel PSD design concept that had just been introduced by Pavlychuk et al.[13–15]. Accordingly several PSD components with different purposes were tailored to work in a sequentially coordinated fashion. A primary reduction/prefixation PSD component was created to catch and stabilize a multitude of medial condylar head fragments within a cage−like framework. The cranial end of this cage carried four terminal phalanges reaching over the domal crest of the reassembled fragments. Although the PSD could, by and large, be accommodated within the fracture site, we failed to advance the extensions across the dome convexity. All attempts led to unresolvable dislodgments and made the application of the following PSD components impossible.

segments.heading: Discussion / Case-specific Insights and Recommendations
segments.text: As a consequence of this misassessment that had its origin in the VSP/CAD phase, we recommend to omit extensions, overhangings or undercuts within morphological transition zones, in order to prevent intraoperative hardware collisions.

segments.heading: Discussion / Case-specific Insights and Recommendations
segments.text: Similar design flaws with increasingly complex PSD have been observed in other settings, e.g., bilateral sagittal split ramus osteotomies with CAD/CAM technology [].
segments.text_with_reference_markers: Similar design flaws with increasingly complex PSD have been observed in other settings, e.g., bilateral sagittal split ramus osteotomies with CAD/CAM technology [ [BIBR:CR16 16] ].

segments.heading: Discussion / Case-specific Insights and Recommendations
segments.text: Our motive to apply PSDs in CHF surgical treatment was the search for simplification and improvement of accuracy. Currently their benefit is not yet sufficiently ascertained; there is a clear need to identify refined indication criteria particularly in multifragmentation fractures. In cases of extremely damaged joints, total joint replacement (TJR) may be considered alternately. While traditionally reserved for end-stage TMJ-pathology, Pruszyńska et al. suggest TJR as primary option for multifragmented CHF if the mandibular ramus height cannot be reliably restored via ORIF [, ].

text:
[b00001] Abstract
Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of condylar head fractures (CHF) can be challenging. Virtual planning and CAD/CAM-based patient-specific devices (PSD) offer to enhance the accuracy of fragment reduction. We present four CHF cases demonstrating the strengths and shortcomings of different PSD designs. From this still limited experience, some fundamental recommendations evolved: • The PSD design should permit adequate visualization of the fracture line to ensure anatomical fracture reduction. • The PSD for reposition and prefixation of the medial fragment should incorporate an abundance of screw holes, particularly in its lateral section, since this part is most easily accessible intraoperatively. • PSDs extended over the dome of the condylar head should be omitted to avoid interferences between fragments, PSD and the adjacent glenoid fossa.

[b00002] Introduction
Mandibular condylar head fractures (CHF) can be treated non-surgically or through open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) []. ORIF is the preferred modality when the CHF lines are located within or below the lateral pole zone of the condyle and accompanied by dislocation of the medial fragment, resulting in loss of the vertical ramus height []. ORIF has been demonstrated to provide superior morphological and functional outcomes compared to non-surgical therapy of CHF [–].

[b00003] Introduction
Various techniques for ORIF of CHF were described in the literature including microplates, miniplates, lag screws and positional screws [–]. Lateral small-fragment positional screw osteosynthesis (LSFPSO) has shown good functional and stable long-term outcomes []. Still, accurate reduction and fixation of the medial bone portions may be demanding above all in major fragmentation [].

[b00004] Introduction
Virtual surgical planning (VSP) and computer-aided design/ computer-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM) PSDs provide high accuracy for reduction of bone segments or fragments and are current best practice in orthognathic surgery and post-trauma or oncologic reconstruction of the facial skeleton [–].

[b00005] Introduction
This case series (from 2017 to 2020) reviews PSDs for ORIF of CHF, analyses their advantages and limitations, and suggests design refinements to overcome identified drawbacks.

[b00006] Case 1
38-year-old male with bilateral mandibular CHF and a symphyseal fracture resulting from interpersonal violence.

[b00007] Case 1 / Clinical Findings
Limited jaw opening, bilateral preauricular swelling, malocclusion, frontal open bite.

[b00008] Case 1 / Imaging and Planning
High-resolution (0.625 mm) Computed Tomography (CT) revealed bilateral CHF, both lateral to the lateral pole zone (AO type-p) (Table 1) with lost vertical apposition, no fragmentation on the right, and minor fragmentation on the left (Fig. 1).

[b00009] Case 1 / Imaging and Planning
Interactive VSP with an industrial partner (KLS Martin Group, Tuttlingen, Germany) went for a PSD design to assist anatomical fracture reduction of the medial condylar fragment and prefixation prior to definitive fixation with a two screw LSFPSO. The PSDs were intended for removal at the operation’s conclusion.

[b00010] Case 1 / Implant Design
The PSD design featured a solid rhomboid shield in the upper part for reduction and prefixation of the medial fragment, transitioning into a curved lower end below the fracture line for fixation along the lateral surface of the ramus. Multiple holes enabled flexibility for optimal screw placement, accommodating emerging access limitations or compromised bone quality.

[b00011] Case 1 / Surgical Procedure
The symphyseal fracture underwent ORIF with two miniplates. The right CHF was exposed through a preauricular approach. The medial condylar fragment, displaced antero-caudo-medially, was reduced by means of sharp hooks and diamond-coated elevators. The placement of the PSD obstructed the fracture line with its rhomboid shield, necessitating a change in strategy. Instead of the PSD a grid plate (1.2 mm screws; Medartis AG, Basel, Switzerland) was used for prefixation of the medial fragment after anatomical reduction. The PSD was then placed onto the plate and mounted (1.2 mm screws) for reinforcement. Two small-fragment screws (1.8 mm, Medartis) were inserted in typical LSFPSO manner. The left-side ORIF with the second PSD was deferred because a reproducible multipoint occlusion had been achieved via reduction of the right condylar head.

[b00012] Case 1 / Outcome
Postoperative Panorex confirmed adequate reduction and fixation. Functional treatment with elastics was performed for three weeks.

[b00013] Case 2
13-year-old boy with a right mandibular CHF caused by a fall.

[b00014] Case 2 / Clinical Findings
Limited jaw opening, contralateral open bite.

[b00015] Case 2 / Imaging and Planning
CT imaging revealed an AO type-p CHF with no fragmentation but lost vertical apposition. The medial fragment exhibited an atypical rectangular shape and was displaced antero-medially and angulated caudally (Fig. 2).

[b00016] Case 2 / Imaging and Planning
VSP mirrored the contralateral condylar head to define the pre-injury position of the fragment as foundation for the PSD design. This approach was comfortable but ignored the unique shape of the medial fragment and the fracture line’s course, eventually leading to suboptimal PSD fit.

[b00017] Case 2 / Implant Design
A P-shaped PSD with three screw holes for dorsal fixation of the medial fragment and additional holes for lateral neck fixation was designed. Angulated insertion points for two positional screws were incorporated. The PSD allowed for visualization of the fracture line; removal at the end of the operation was planned.

[b00018] Case 2 / Surgical Procedure
The PSD bridged the fracture. The fragment’s flat configuration allowed LSFPSO with one screw (1.8 mm, length:15 mm; Medartis) only. Consequently, the PSD was left in situ as stand-by to reinforce overall stability.

[b00019] Case 2 / Outcome
Postoperative CT confirmed proper reduction and fixation.

[b00020] Case 2 / Outcome
Elastics were used for 10 days. At seven months postoperatively, bony consolidation was observed, though screw and plate loosening necessitated hardware removal. Preinjury occlusion was stable, and jaw opening unrestricted.

[b00021] Case 3
59-year-old woman after right CHF, initially treated non-surgically.

[b00022] Case 3 / Clinical Findings
Malocclusion, right temporomandibular joint pain 16 months post injury.

[b00023] Case 3 / Imaging and Planning
Imaging revealed deformation of the right condylar head with vertical ramus height loss due to medial fragment displacement (Fig. 3). VSP led to the implementation of a crescent-shaped osteotomy for mobilization and reduction of the medial segment and PSD-assisted fixation. The virtual reduction of the medial fragment produced an osteotomy gap.

[b00024] Case 3 / Implant Design
Due to this gap a large-scale, rigid P-shaped PSD was designed with a fenestration to inspect the osteotomy gap, multiple screw holes for bony anchoring and LSFPSO indicators. The upper arm contained 3 screw receiving holes. The lower arm descended on the posterior surface of the condylar process with a curvature below the level of the sigmoid notch to create enough space for five screw holes. The principal load bearing function relied on the LSFPSO. The optimal entry points for two respective screws were indicated by triangular laser-etched notches in the lower arm of the PSD.

[b00025] Case 3 / Surgical Procedure
A piezosurgery osteotomy was performed, and the medial condylar segment was repositioned into the glenoid fossa. The PSD was applied uneventfully. Owing to poor bone quality, prefixation of the medial segment with a screw was limited to the uppermost PSD hole. As anticipated an irregular gap remained between the segments. The upper screw for the LSPSO could be inserted guided by the notch indicator. Since the form of the bony gap differed from VSP due to the material reduction during piezosurgical sawing the second screw was inserted free hand antero-superiorly of the indicating notch and angulated in a vertical direction to safely purchase the medial fragment.

[b00026] Case 3 / Outcome
X-rays confirmed adequate reduction of the condylar head, proper location in the glenoid fossa and restored vertical ramus height.

[b00027] Case 3 / Outcome
Six months postoperatively, the patient developed right-sided preauricular pain and restricted jaw opening. CT-Imaging revealed a contact of the PSD with the glenoid fossa. Hardware removal alleviated symptoms, and further follow-up was unremarkable.

[b00028] Case 4
62-year-old man with left mandibular multi-fragmented CHF following a bike accident.

[b00029] Case 4 / Clinical Findings
Severe occlusal disturbances, ipsilateral open bite.

[b00030] Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
CT-Scans delineated a left AO type-p CHF with multi-fragmentation (three major fragments), loss of vertical apposition, and anteromedial displacement (Fig. 4).

[b00031] Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
A three-component multi-purpose PSD was designed. In line with previous cases, one PSD component of the PSD was designated to reduction and prefixation. To address the difficulties in stabilizing the dislocated largest medial fragment alongside smaller pieces, the upper PSD portion was equipped with four finger-like extensions along the entire posterior surface of the condylar head. The middle section of the PSD incorporated a large window for unobstructed visualization of the fracture line and its cranial ramifications. The lower PSD portion encompassed the neck region, reaching down to the level of the deepest point of the sigmoid notch. Its anterior border contained an undulating recess serving as docking site for the second PSD component, i.e. a “tandem” washer for load distribution and reinforcement of the LSFPSO.

[b00032] Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
The upper PSD portion included six screw holes arranged in two rows (four along the common arch brace and one on each of the two central dome extensions) to ensure adequate fixation of the reassembled fragments, even if not every screw hole was occupied. The lower PSD portion contained three screw holes in a triangular configuration for anchoring to the condylar neck and base region.

[b00033] Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
The PSD “tandem” washer seated within the lateral recess along the first PSD component. This second PSD combined washer and navigation function: the tongue-in-groove design of the two components ensured accurate intraoperative transfer of the LSFPSO entry points onto the lateral fracture end at the ramus. Besides the two washer screw holes the PSD contained a third smaller hole for its temporary fixation during LSFPSO.

[b00034] Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
Detachable drill guides, designed to indicate the angulation and intramedullary pathways for the LSFPSO screws within the medial fragment assembly, were provided in two versions: two separate metallic cylinders joined by a polymer sleeve with and without a long rod-like handle.

[b00035] Case 4 / Imaging and Planning
The PSD tool set was complemented with a third component, a small T-shaped implant to augment the rigidity of the overall reconstruction after removal of the primary (reduction/prefixation) PSD. The T-shaped PSD was conceived to link the condylar neck and head and retain the small intermediate dorsal monocortical fragment (SIDMF) at the posterior condylar surface.

[b00036] Case 4 / Surgical Procedure
The dislocated major dome fragment, along with the smaller medial fragments, were successfully reassembled and anatomically reduced. However, repeated attempts to position the reduction/prefixation PSD component as pre-planned failed. Unresolvable collisions between the dome fragment, the cranial PSD extensions and the glenoid fossa hindered the first component from bypassing the bony crest and slipping into its planned final position.

[b00037] Case 4 / Surgical Procedure
For salvage the large medial condylar head fragment was reduced and fixated to the lateral fracture end with a conventional grid plate (1.2 mm screws; Medartis). To achieve this, it became necessary to remove the SIDMF and to close the interfragmentary gap by a slight pitch movement. This adjustment was required because the available grid plate was too short.

[b00038] Case 4 / Surgical Procedure
The entry points for the LSFPSO were established with the aid of the washer PSD. Despite the discrepancies from VSP, the placement of the washer components, drill guides and drilling could be carried out with sufficient precision. Because the bone surrounding the drill holes did not necessitate load distribution the washer PSD was removed prior to insertion of two screws (1.8 mm screws; Medartis) for the LSFPSO.

[b00039] Case 4 / Surgical Procedure
Occlusion and latero-/protrusion movements were assessed intraoperatively and confirmed satisfactory fracture reduction and stabilisation. Consequently, the grid plate was removed. Minimisation of the residual gap and SIDMF replantation were deemed unnecessary. Further stabilization with the T-shaped PSD was also not pursued.

[b00040] Case 4 / Outcome
A postoperative panoramic X-ray confirmed anatomical reduction of the fracture.

[b00041] Case 4 / Outcome
Clinical Follow up: asymptomatic with unimpaired function.

[b00042] Discussion
LSFPSO using two or three screws has emerged as the most popular surgical treatment modality for CHF [, ]. The concept of combining PSDs with screw fixation might offer a promising approach for treating challenging CHF up to most troublesome multifragment patterns [].

[b00043] Discussion
Pavlychuk et al. have outlined sophisticated CAD/CAM PSD designs to support ORIF of CHFs across three publications [–]. For unclear reasons, their concept has not met much resonance in the literature so far. Our case series showcases the intraoperative constraints encountered with three single-component and one multi-component PSD, the latter inspired by Pavlychuk et al.

[b00044] Discussion / Roles and Advantages of PSD in CHFs
PSDs are used alongside LSFPSO. PSDs can be tailored to perform multiple functions, including:

[b00045] Discussion / Roles and Advantages of PSD in CHFs
Assist reduction, reassembly and prefixation of medial condylar head fragments. Navigate LSFPSO entry points. Guide drilling for intramedullary screw placement (LSFPSO). Augment osteosynthesis rigidity through reinforcement.

[b00046] Discussion / Roles and Advantages of PSD in CHFs
PSDs may be employed intraoperatively only or retained for long-term stability. Their advantages over off-the-shelf hardware include improved fragment reduction accuracy, enhanced rigidity, and reduced operative time, as evidenced in other surgical contexts [, ].

[b00047] Discussion / Insights from this Case Series
A principal cause for the pitfalls described above was limited experience with nuanced PSD design features for CHF management. Crucially, salvage solutions were at hand in all cases. To flatten the learning curve in order to establish and help to disseminate PSDs in surgical CHF treatment, we would like to refer to the following recommendations and caveats for the PSD design:

[b00048] Discussion / Insights from this Case Series
VSP–Fracture Line Analysis: Accurate analysis of the fracture line and reduction of fragments in the planning phase is essential – rather than simply relying on mirroring and superimposition of intact contralateral structures. Mandibular asymmetry will compromise the true morphology and course of fracture lines []. Intraoperative Visualization: Ensure a reliable overview of the entire fracture line course during every phase of the surgical intervention by incorporating large fenestrations or cross-bracings into the PSD design. This principle has been repeatedly exemplified in wire-frame patient-specific cutting guides [, ]. Flexible Strategies for Screw Fixation: Provide an excess of drilling/ screw−receiving holes in the PSD design, even if only the most suitable subset of the surplus of screw holes may be occupied to deal with unforeseen problems, such as poor bone quality or inaccessible anatomic sites. The integration of screw holes in excess numbers into osteosynthesis plates designs to increase intraoperative flexibility has already been described in context with condylar base and neck fractures []. Thoughtfully executed Coverage across Relevant Anatomical Sites: Extend the PSD to encompass the infero−lateral surface of the medial condylar head fragment approaching to the margin of the fracture line. This is an easily accessible area, which facilitates screw insertion besides control of accurate reduction of the inferior part of the fracture. Temporary Use of Grid Plates: Remove grid plates or medial fragment−reduction PSD component after LSFPSO is secured unless a “stand−by” stabilization is required.

[b00049] Discussion / Insights from this Case Series
Loosening of positional screws and conventional grid plates is a known issue in ORIF of CHF []. Possible causes include poor bone quality or cyclic loading, leading to the backout of screws []. Therefore, a grid plate or PSD should be removed subsequent to the LSFPSO to preclude a secondary hardware removal. An exception is the need for additional stabilization via “standby” with extrabony fixation devices.

[b00050] Discussion / Case-specific Insights and Recommendations
At the treatment time of Case 4, we have been overly enthusiastic in adopting ideas from the novel PSD design concept that had just been introduced by Pavlychuk et al.[13–15]. Accordingly several PSD components with different purposes were tailored to work in a sequentially coordinated fashion. A primary reduction/prefixation PSD component was created to catch and stabilize a multitude of medial condylar head fragments within a cage−like framework. The cranial end of this cage carried four terminal phalanges reaching over the domal crest of the reassembled fragments. Although the PSD could, by and large, be accommodated within the fracture site, we failed to advance the extensions across the dome convexity. All attempts led to unresolvable dislodgments and made the application of the following PSD components impossible.

[b00051] Discussion / Case-specific Insights and Recommendations
As a consequence of this misassessment that had its origin in the VSP/CAD phase, we recommend to omit extensions, overhangings or undercuts within morphological transition zones, in order to prevent intraoperative hardware collisions.

[b00052] Discussion / Case-specific Insights and Recommendations
Similar design flaws with increasingly complex PSD have been observed in other settings, e.g., bilateral sagittal split ramus osteotomies with CAD/CAM technology [].

[b00053] Discussion / Case-specific Insights and Recommendations
Our motive to apply PSDs in CHF surgical treatment was the search for simplification and improvement of accuracy. Currently their benefit is not yet sufficiently ascertained; there is a clear need to identify refined indication criteria particularly in multifragmentation fractures. In cases of extremely damaged joints, total joint replacement (TJR) may be considered alternately. While traditionally reserved for end-stage TMJ-pathology, Pruszyńska et al. suggest TJR as primary option for multifragmented CHF if the mandibular ramus height cannot be reliably restored via ORIF [, ].
